newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope begins private mountain retreat in Italy Alps.
newsitem.headline: Pope begins private mountain retreat in Italy Alps.

text.p: A cheerful but somewhat tired looking Pope John Paul began a 10-day private mountain holiday on Wednesday to relax midway through a hectic year in which he has already made four overseas trips.

"I wish you all good holidays," the 77-year-old Pontiff told a small group of children and other well-wishers who gathered on a clearing to watch him arrive by helicopter in the Val D'Aosta region near the French border.
The Pope used a cane to walk across the field where the helicopter landed. He appeared weary but in good spirits, stopping to chat with a group of priests and local authorities.
He smiled as he spoke with residents, including a Polish woman who married a local man and taught the Polish refrain Sto Lat (may you live 100 years) to schoolchildren who sang it on his arrival.
But the leader of the world's Roman Catholics apparently did not feel up to walking part way to a stone and wooden chalet where he will be billeted, as he had done in recent years.

The chalet, adjacent to a church-owned retreat outside the isolated hamlet of Les Combes, has a view of the snow-capped Mont Blanc, at 4,880 metres (16,000 Feet) Europe's tallest mountain, and alpine glaciers.
From the 1300-metre (4,300 feet) high chalet the Pope will take short walks and leave for alpine outings. But aides say he will spend much of his time relaxing and reading.

The Pope was an avid mountaineer until he broke his leg in a fall in the Vatican in 1994 and underwent hip replacement surgery. He has since walked with difficulty and has needed the help of a cane to negotiate unfamiliar ground.
The Pope has had a series of health problems in recent years. Ten months ago he underwent surgery to remove an inflamed appendix. The Vatican says his overall health is good.
The Vatican has said the mountain retreat will be strictly private. The only public engagement will be on Sunday when the Pope recites his weekly blessing from the balcony of the chalet.

Vatican officials said the Pope will use the 10 days to catch up on reading literature and work on texts of speeches he will make during his next trip abroad, a four-day visit to Paris to celebrate the Roman Catholic Church's World Day of Youth.
The Pope broke with centuries of tradition in 1986 when he began taking holidays outside the papal summer retreat at Castelgandolfo, south of Rome.
The Pontiff has made four trips abroad this year -- to Sarajevo, Lebanon, the Czech Republic and his native Poland. He is due to visit Paris in August and Brazil in October.
